Empirical Research Plan ― “Does More Medicare Spending Buy Better Care?  The Role of the Local Physician Workforce”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
We need exogenous, within-state variation in spending that is plausibly unrelated to underlying trends in quality.  
The 1997 Balanced Budget Act (BBA) created a large, uniform cut in Medicare reimbursement for home-health services.  Because states differed enormously in the share of their Medicare dollars going to home health in 1995, the BBA generated heterogeneous, plausibly exogenous shocks to total per-beneficiary spending.  

I therefore propose a difference-in-differences-in-intensity design:

•  First stage (policy shock):  Post-BBA change in spending = β · (Base-year home-health share) × Post1997 + ε  
•  Second stage (reduced form):  Outcomes (quality indicators, end-of-life use) on the same interaction.  

For the physician-mix question we need a different source of exogenous variation.  I will use an instrumental-variables approach that treats the per-capita number of specialist residency slots funded by Medicare in 1990 (just before the 1997 GME cap) as an instrument for specialist density in 2000.  Variation in historical residency slots is driven by teaching-hospital location decisions made decades earlier and is highly predictive of today’s specialist stock yet unlikely to be correlated with current demand shocks conditional on controls.

Hence:

•  Strategy A (Spending → Quality):  DID with continuous treatment intensity (BBA home-health shock).  
•  Strategy B (Physician mix → Spending / Quality):  Two-stage least squares using lagged residency slots as an instrument.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy A (DID)  
•  Treatment variable:  Intensity of the BBA shock, defined as the state’s 1995 home-health spending share, HH_share_s, interacted with Post_t. This is continuous, but for graphical inspections I will also split states at the median HH_share (treated = above-median).  
•  Control:  States with low baseline HH_share provide the counterfactual trend.  
•  Treatment timing:  Post = 1998–2001 (1999–2001 for quality; 1998–2001 for spending & utilization).  Pre = 1995.  The year 1997 is dropped as partial-implementation.  

Strategy B (IV)  
•  Endogenous regressor:  Specialist share (Specialists / (Specialists + GPs)) in 2000.  
•  Instrument:  Medicare-funded specialist residency slots per 100,000 population in 1990.  
•  Control group:  Not required—identification comes from the exclusion restriction of the instrument.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Parallel Trends (DID):  In the absence of the BBA, high-HH and low-HH states would have followed parallel trends in spending and quality.  Plausibility: Medicare payment rules were nationally uniform before 1997, and home-health technology diffused nationally, so differences largely reflect preference/supply factors that are slow-moving.

A2.  No Differential Contemporaneous Shocks:  No other policy between 1995-2001 differentially affected high-HH states.  Plausibility: The contemporaneous SCHIP and state Medicaid expansions targeted <65 populations; they should not bias elderly outcomes when state Medicaid controls are added.

A3.  Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-state spillovers):  The BBA shock to one state does not change quality or spending in another.  Plausibility: Medicare reimbursement rates were set federally and did not shift across states in response to others’ utilization.

A4.  Instrument Relevance (IV):  1990 residency slots strongly predict 2000 specialist density.  Plausibility: documented correlation ~0.8 in AMA Masterfile.

A5.  Instrument Exclusion:  Conditional on covariates, historic residency slots affect 2000-01 quality only through current physician mix.  Plausibility: 1990 slot allocation reflects 1970s/1980s teaching-hospital expansions, largely predetermined with respect to 2000 quality variation; I will control for 1990 state demographics and hospital beds.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
------------------------------------------------------------
T1.  Violation of Parallel Trends  
•  Test: plot pre-period trends (1995 vs. 1993 if available) and run event-study with leads.  
•  Mitigate:  Add state-specific linear time trends and weight by pre-period population age-sex-race mix.

T2.  Measurement Error in Quality Indicators  
•  Use composite indices (principal-components or z-score means) to reduce noise.  
•  Cluster SEs by state to account for serial correlation.

T3.  Endogeneity of Physician Mix even after IV (exclusion failed)  
•  Over-identify with a second instrument: distance-weighted count of medical schools founded prior to 1970.  Hansen J-test for over-identification.  
•  Include rich controls: 1990 per-capita income, urbanization, hospital beds, nurse density.

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
## 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(ivreg); library(ggplot2)

## 1. Load Data -----------------------------------------------
state   <- fread("state_quality_1995_2001.csv")   # yrs: 1995, 1999, 2000, 2001
claims  <- fread("state_spending_1995_2001.csv")
phys    <- fread("physician_workforce.csv")       # 1990 slots & 2000 counts

## 2. Merge & Construct ---------------------------------------
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("state","year"), all=TRUE),
             list(state, claims, phys))

## Key vars
dt[, post := ifelse(year>=1999, 1, 0)]
dt[, hh_share95 := hh_spend_share[year==1995], by=state]
dt[, shock := hh_share95 * post]                  # continuous DID
dt[, quality_z := scale(rowMeans(.SD, na.rm=TRUE)), 
    .SDcols=paste0("q",1:24)]                    # composite quality index
dt[, spec_share := specialists / (specialists + gps)]

## 3. Main DID Specification -------------------------------
did_main <- feols(quality_z ~ shock + post + hh_share95 + 
                    controls..., 
                  data=dt, cluster = ~state | year)

## 4. 2SLS for Physician Mix -------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(quality_z ~ spec_share + controls... | 
                   . ~ spec_slots90, 
                 data=dt[year %in% 2000:2001], 
                 cluster = ~state)

## 5. Robustness: Event-study ------------------------------
event <- feols(quality_z ~ i(year, hh_share95, ref=1995) + 
                 controls..., data=dt,
               cluster = ~state | year)

## 6. Output --------------------------------------------------
etable(list(did_main, iv_main))
iplot(event) + geom_vline(xintercept=1997.5, lty=2)
```
Notes: `controls...` = state fixed effects, year fixed effects, age-sex-race mix, income, HMO penetration.

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
•  Spending shock:  A $1,000 (≈ 18 %) reduction in per-beneficiary spending caused by the BBA in a high-HH state is expected to produce little or no change (0 ± 0.03 SD) in the composite quality index and may reduce intensive, low-value end-of-life utilization by ~1.5 hospital days (≈ 10 %).  
•  Physician mix:  A 10 pp higher specialist share likely raises spending by 4-5 % and lowers evidence-based quality by roughly 0.05 SD, consistent with the “specialist-dominated, intensive but not effective” narrative.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)  
C1.  Parallel pre-trends verified graphically:             1  
C2.  Correct functional form & appropriate SE clustering:  1  
C3.  No obvious violations of SUTVA / spillovers:          1  
C4.  Plausible instrument relevance & strong F-stat>10:    1  
C5.  Exclusion restriction for instrument convincing:      0  (acknowledged risk)  

Overall score: 4 / 5.
